books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate

stimulus.text:
The table shows the share of eligible voters who cast ballots in presidential elections, 
from 1824 to 1840, as recorded by the U.S. Bureau of the Census.
| Year | Share of eligible voters who voted |
| 1824 | 26.9% |
| 1828 | 57.6% |
| 1832 | 55.4% |
| 1836 | 57.8% |
| 1840 | 80.2% |
stimulus.source_note: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The change in turnout between 1824 and 1828 best reflects which development?

options.text: Women won the vote in most states
options.misconception: Women did not win the vote in this period; the new voters were white men.

options.text: The electorate shrank as states added property rules
options.misconception: States were dropping property rules, and the electorate grew, not shrank.

options.text: Political parties disappeared after the Era of Good Feelings
options.misconception: Parties did not disappear; Jackson's Democrats and their rivals organized mass campaigns.

options.text: Suffrage expanded and mass parties campaigned for the new voters

rationales.A: Women did not gain the vote in the 1820s.
rationales.B: The electorate grew as property rules fell; it did not shrink.
rationales.C: Parties grew stronger in the 1820s, they did not vanish.
rationales.D: Property rules fell in the 1820s while Jackson's campaign turned the “corrupt bargain” charge into a mass appeal, so turnout more than doubled.
rationales.general:
1. Measure the jump. Turnout rose from 26.9 percent in 1824 to 57.6 percent in 1828, more than doubling.
2. Find the new voters. Most states had dropped property qualifications, so most free white men could vote.
3. Find the pull. Jackson's campaign against the “corrupt bargain” gave those new voters a reason to come out.
Background: In 1800 only five states let voters choose presidential electors directly; by 1824, 18 of 24 did.
Remember: turnout jumps when new voters meet a campaign that wants them.
